claim: The majority of human breast cancer is estrogen receptor alpha (ER) positive.
source: The majority of human breast cancer is estrogen receptor alpha (ER) positive.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of breast cancer research, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Resistance to anti-estrogens and aromatase inhibitors commonly develops in breast cancer treatment.
source: While anti-estrogens/aromatase inhibitors are initially effective, resistance to these drugs commonly develops.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about breast cancer treatment resistance.

claim: Therapy-resistant tumors often retain ER signaling via interaction with critical oncogenic coregulator proteins.
source: Therapy-resistant tumors often retain ER signaling, via interaction with critical oncogenic coregulator proteins.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited in the introduction section.

claim: ERX-11 is a novel ER coregulator binding modulator.
source: To address these mechanisms of resistance, we have developed a novel ER coregulator binding modulator, ERX-11.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ERX-11 interacts directly with ER.
source: ERX-11 interacts directly with ER and blocks the interaction between a subset of coregulators with both native and mutant forms of ER.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pulldown assays, mass spectrometry, and binding studies shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: ERX-11 blocks the interaction between ER and a subset of coregulators.
source: ERX-11 interacts directly with ER and blocks the interaction between a subset of coregulators with both native and mutant forms of ER.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation, proximity ligation assays, and mass spectrometry data in Figure 2.

claim: ERX-11 blocks interactions with both native and mutant forms of ER.
source: ERX-11 interacts directly with ER and blocks the interaction between a subset of coregulators with both native and mutant forms of ER.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with ER mutants (L540Q, Δ12, Y537S, D538G) shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: ERX-11 effectively blocks ER-mediated oncogenic signaling.
source: ERX-11 effectively blocks ER-mediated oncogenic signaling and has potent anti-proliferative activity against therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNA-seq analysis, pathway analysis, and reporter assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: ERX-11 has potent anti-proliferative activity against therapy-sensitive human breast cancer cells.
source: ERX-11 effectively blocks ER-mediated oncogenic signaling and has potent anti-proliferative activity against therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assays in multiple ER-positive cell lines shown in Figure 1.

claim: ERX-11 has potent anti-proliferative activity against therapy-resistant human breast cancer cells.
source: ERX-11 effectively blocks ER-mediated oncogenic signaling and has potent anti-proliferative activity against therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with tamoxifen-resistant, letrozole-resistant, and HER2-overexpressing cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: ERX-11 is orally bioavailable.
source: ERX-11 is orally bioavailable, with no overt signs of toxicity and potent activity in both murine xenograft and patient-derived breast tumor explant models.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oral gavage administration in mouse studies shown in Figure 5.

claim: ERX-11 shows no overt signs of toxicity in animal models.
source: ERX-11 is orally bioavailable, with no overt signs of toxicity and potent activity in both murine xenograft and patient-derived breast tumor explant models.
evidence: This is supported by toxicity studies in mice showing no weight loss, uterotrophic effects, or organ damage as described in the Results section and Figure 5 supplements.

claim: ERX-11 has potent activity in murine xenograft models.
source: ERX-11 is orally bioavailable, with no overt signs of toxicity and potent activity in both murine xenograft and patient-derived breast tumor explant models.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth inhibition studies in ZR-75, D2A1, MCF-7-PELP1, MCF-7-LTLT, and ZR-75-Y537S xenografts shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: ERX-11 has potent activity in patient-derived breast tumor explant models.
source: ERX-11 is orally bioavailable, with no overt signs of toxicity and potent activity in both murine xenograft and patient-derived breast tumor explant models.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ex vivo culture experiments with primary patient tumors showing reduced proliferation in ER-positive tumors as shown in Figure 7.

claim: ERX-11 overcomes limitations of current therapies through its novel mechanism of disrupting critical protein-protein interactions.
source: This first-in-class agent, with its novel mechanism of action of disrupting critical protein-protein interactions, overcomes the limitations of current therapies and may be clinically translatable for patients with therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant breast cancers.
evidence: This is supported by the demonstration of activity in therapy-resistant models and the unique mechanism of blocking coregulator interactions shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: ERX-11 may be clinically translatable for patients with therapy-sensitive breast cancers.
source: This first-in-class agent, with its novel mechanism of action of disrupting critical protein-protein interactions, overcomes the limitations of current therapies and may be clinically translatable for patients with therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant breast cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the preclinical data presented, including efficacy in multiple models and patient-derived explants.

claim: ERX-11 may be clinically translatable for patients with therapy-resistant breast cancers.
source: This first-in-class agent, with its novel mechanism of action of disrupting critical protein-protein interactions, overcomes the limitations of current therapies and may be clinically translatable for patients with therapy-sensitive and therapy-resistant breast cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the preclinical data showing activity in therapy-resistant models.

claim: Most patients with ER-positive breast cancer develop resistance to endocrine therapies.
source: However, most patients develop resistance to these drugs, and disease progression is common, with progression to metastases (Musgrove and Sutherland, 2009; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ER signaling involves coregulators.
source: ER signaling is complex and involves coregulators (McDonnell and Norris, 2002; O'Malley and Kumar, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Therapy-resistant tumors often retain ER-expression and ER-signaling.
source: Therapy-resistant tumors often retain ER-expression and ER-signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of breast cancer research.

claim: ER signaling in therapy-resistant tumors is mediated by interactions between activated ER and critical coregulator proteins.
source: While multiple mechanisms maintain ER signaling in therapy-resistant tumors, ER signaling is mediated by the interactions between activated ER and critical coregulator proteins (Dasgupta and O'Malley, 2014; Lonard et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Alterations in the concentration or activity of selective coregulators enable ER-signaling from AE-ER complexes, effectively converting the antagonist to an agonist.
source: Alterations in the concentration or activity of selective coregulators enable ER-signaling from AE-ER complexes, effectively converting the antagonist to an agonist (O'Hara et al., 2012; Kurebayashi, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Over a third (38%) of ER coregulators identified in breast cancer are over-expressed.
source: Over a third (38%) of ER coregulators identified in breast cancer are over-expressed (Lonard et al., 2007; Lonard and O'Malley, 2012; Cortez et al., 2014), such as SRC3 (AIB1) (List et al., 2001; Azorsa et al., 2001), SRC2 (Kurebayashi et al., 2000), and PELP1 (Habashy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: SRC3 (AIB1) is over-expressed in breast cancer.
source: Over a third (38%) of ER coregulators identified in breast cancer are over-expressed (Lonard et al., 2007; Lonard and O'Malley, 2012; Cortez et al., 2014), such as SRC3 (AIB1) (List et al., 2001; Azorsa et al., 2001), SRC2 (Kurebayashi et al., 2000), and PELP1 (Habashy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SRC2 is over-expressed in breast cancer.
source: Over a third (38%) of ER coregulators identified in breast cancer are over-expressed (Lonard et al., 2007; Lonard and O'Malley, 2012; Cortez et al., 2014), such as SRC3 (AIB1) (List et al., 2001; Azorsa et al., 2001), SRC2 (Kurebayashi et al., 2000), and PELP1 (Habashy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PELP1 is over-expressed in breast cancer.
source: Over a third (38%) of ER coregulators identified in breast cancer are over-expressed (Lonard et al., 2007; Lonard and O'Malley, 2012; Cortez et al., 2014), such as SRC3 (AIB1) (List et al., 2001; Azorsa et al., 2001), SRC2 (Kurebayashi et al., 2000), and PELP1 (Habashy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Deregulated coregulators contribute to mammary tumorigenesis.
source: These deregulated coregulators contribute to mammary tumorigenesis (Cortez et al., 2014), therapy resistance and metastases (Kumar et al., 2009; Shou et al., 2004; Burandt et al., 2013; Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Deregulated coregulators contribute to therapy resistance.
source: These deregulated coregulators contribute to mammary tumorigenesis (Cortez et al., 2014), therapy resistance and metastases (Kumar et al., 2009; Shou et al., 2004; Burandt et al., 2013; Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Deregulated coregulators contribute to metastases.
source: These deregulated coregulators contribute to mammary tumorigenesis (Cortez et al., 2014), therapy resistance and metastases (Kumar et al., 2009; Shou et al., 2004; Burandt et al., 2013; Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Breast tumors acquire mutations in the ER ligand binding domains (L536N, Y537S, Y537N and D538G) that facilitate constitutive activity of these mutant ER in the absence of ligand.
source: Recent studies revealed that breast tumors acquire mutations in the ER ligand binding domains (L536N, Y537S, Y537N and D538G) that facilitate constitutive activity of these mutant ER (MT-ER) in the absence of ligand (Toy et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Tumors with MT-ER interact with oncogenic coregulators to drive ER-dependent transcriptional programs and proliferation.
source: Tumors with MT-ER interact with oncogenic coregulators to drive ER-dependent transcriptional programs and proliferation and are poorly responsive to AEs and AIs (Toy et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumors with MT-ER are poorly responsive to AEs and AIs.
source: Tumors with MT-ER interact with oncogenic coregulators to drive ER-dependent transcriptional programs and proliferation and are poorly responsive to AEs and AIs (Toy et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The peptidomimetic D2 blocks the interaction between the androgen receptor (AR) and NR-box containing coregulators, such as PELP1, with an IC50 of 40 nM.
source: The peptidomimetic D2 blocks the interaction between the androgen receptor (AR) and NR-box containing coregulators, such as PELP1, with an IC50 of 40 nM (Ravindranathan et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: String analyses of the PELP1 interactome suggested an equally robust interaction between PELP1 and ER as that between PELP1 and AR.
source: String analyses of the PELP1 interactome suggested an equally robust interaction between PELP1 and ER as that between PELP1 and AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: D2 was unable to block the interaction between PELP1 and ER.
source: However, D2 was unable to block the interaction between PELP1 and ER (data not shown) and required much higher concentrations (µM range) to block the proliferation of ER-driven MCF-7 breast cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: D2 required much higher concentrations (µM range) to block the proliferation of ER-driven MCF-7 breast cancer cells.
source: However, D2 was unable to block the interaction between PELP1 and ER (data not shown) and required much higher concentrations (µM range) to block the proliferation of ER-driven MCF-7 breast cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sequences flanking the NR-box may influence the affinity and selectivity of coregulator interactions.
source: Since sequences flanking the NR-box may influence the affinity and selectivity of coregulator interactions (McInerney et al., 1998), we hypothesized that a longer oligo-benzamide scaffold may more effectively target the interaction between ER and coregulators.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature and forms the basis for the design strategy.

claim: A series of tris-benzamides (ERXs) were synthesized that added a functional group (R) to the D2 bis-benzamide, corresponding to the amino acid side chain groups found at the i-3/4 or i + 7 position surrounding the NR-box sequences.
source: This strategy generated a series of tris-benzamides (see Appendix 1—chemical structures 1—22) (Figure 1A) that added a functional group (R) to the D2 bis-benzamide, corresponding to the amino acid side chain groups found at the i-3/4 or i + 7 position surrounding the NR-box sequences (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the chemical structures shown in Figure 1A and synthesis schemes in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Each of the ERXs had differential activities in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
source: Importantly, each of these small molecules were named as ER coregulator binding modulators (ERXs, where X refers to their multiple potential and unknown targets) had differential activities in ER-positive breast cancer cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), confirming our hypothesis that the sequences flanking the core LXXLL motif could determine specificity and activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The sequences flanking the core LXXLL motif determine specificity and activity of ERXs.
source: Importantly, each of these small molecules were named as ER coregulator binding modulators (ERXs, where X refers to their multiple potential and unknown targets) had differential activities in ER-positive breast cancer cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), confirming our hypothesis that the sequences flanking the core LXXLL motif could determine specificity and activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential activities of ERXs with different flanking groups shown in the data.

claim: The ERXs maintained the structural requirement for mimicking helices.
source: The ERXs maintained the structural requirement for mimicking helices (confirmed by molecular modeling (MacroModel, Schrodinger, NY) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, shown for ERX-11).
evidence: This is supported by molecular modeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ERX-11 has a hydroxyethyl functional group mimicking a serine residue.
source: Within this series of tris-benzamides, one compound (ERX-11) with a hydroxyethyl functional group mimicking a serine residue (Figure 1A) was consistently able to block 17-β-estradiol (E2)-induced proliferation in 8/8 ER-positive breast cancer cell lines (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1C, D and 2B), with an IC50, ranging from 250 to 500 nM.
evidence: This is shown in the chemical structure in Figure 1A.

claim: ERX-11 was consistently able to block E2-induced proliferation in 8/8 ER-positive breast cancer cell lines with an IC50 ranging from 250 to 500 nM.
source: Within this series of tris-benzamides, one compound (ERX-11) with a hydroxyethyl functional group mimicking a serine residue (Figure 1A) was consistently able to block 17-β-estradiol (E2)-induced proliferation in 8/8 ER-positive breast cancer cell lines (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1C, D and 2B), with an IC50, ranging from 250 to 500 nM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assays shown in Figure 1B and supplements.

claim: ERX-11 had no effect in 11/12 ER-negative cells, with modest activity in the MDA-MB-157 cell line.
source: In contrast, no effect of ERX-11 was noted in 11/12 ER-negative cells, with modest activity in the MDA-MB-157 cell line (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ERX-11 was as effective as tamoxifen or ICI in reducing the growth of ZR-75 and MCF-7 cells.
source: ERX-11 was as effective as tamoxifen or ICI in reducing the growth of ZR-75 and MCF-7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and 2C,D,E), and the combination of ERX-11 and tamoxifen was not additive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and 2C,D,E.

claim: The combination of ERX-11 and tamoxifen was not additive.
source: ERX-11 was as effective as tamoxifen or ICI in reducing the growth of ZR-75 and MCF-7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplements 1E and 2C,D,E), and the combination of ERX-11 and tamoxifen was not additive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by combination treatment assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Modeling studies using Autodock indicated that ERX-11 could bind to the AF-2 domain of ER.
source: Modeling studies using Autodock (The Scripps Research Institute, La Jolla, CA) indicated that ERX-11 could bind to the AF-2 domain of ER (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by computational docking studies shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Biotinylated ERX-11 interacts with purified ER protein in vitro.
source: Using biotinylated ERX-11 (synthesis described in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), we showed that ERX-11 interacts in vitro with purified ER protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Addition of 'cold' ERX-11 efficiently competed for the binding of purified ER protein to biotinylated ERX-11.
source: Addition of 'cold' ERX-11 efficiently competed for the binding of purified ER protein to biotinylated ERX-11 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Short 15mer peptides corresponding to NR box sequences within the SRC1, SRC2, AIB1 and PELP1 proteins efficiently disrupted the interaction between biotinylated ERX-11 and purified ER.
source: Further, short 15mer peptides, corresponding to NR box sequences within the SRC1, SRC2, AIB1 and PELP1 proteins, efficiently disrupted the interaction between biotinylated ERX-11 and purified ER (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays with LXXLL peptides shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Not all LXXLL peptides interfere with ERX-11 interaction with ER, as only peptide surrounding the third PELP1 LXXLL motif, but not the first PELP1 LXXLL motif blocked ERX-11 interaction.
source: However, not all LXXLL peptides interfere ERX-11 interaction with ER, as only peptide surrounding the third PELP1 LXXLL motif, but not the first PELP1 LXXLL motif blocked ERX-11 interaction suggesting ERX-11 can only block some LXXLL interactions (Figure 1G, last two panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by selective competition with different PELP1 LXXLL peptides shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ERX-11 can only block some LXXLL interactions.
source: However, not all LXXLL peptides interfere ERX-11 interaction with ER, as only peptide surrounding the third PELP1 LXXLL motif, but not the first PELP1 LXXLL motif blocked ERX-11 interaction suggesting ERX-11 can only block some LXXLL interactions (Figure 1G, last two panels).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective competition data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Pre-incubation of purified ER protein with SERDs GDC-0810 or AZD-9496, or fulvestrant (ICI) was unable to block the interaction between ER and ERX-11.
source: Further, pre-incubation of the purified ER protein with selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs) GDC-0810 or AZD-9496, or fulvestrant (ICI) was unable to block the interaction between ER and ERX-11 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Tamoxifen was able to block the interaction between purified ER and ERX-11.
source: In contrast, tamoxifen was able to block the interaction between purified ER and ERX-11 (Figure 1H), suggesting similarities in the ER-binding pockets of ERX-11 and tamoxifen.
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There are similarities in the ER-binding pockets of ERX-11 and tamoxifen.
source: In contrast, tamoxifen was able to block the interaction between purified ER and ERX-11 (Figure 1H), suggesting similarities in the ER-binding pockets of ERX-11 and tamoxifen.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition data showing tamoxifen can block ERX-11 binding.

claim: Biotinylated ERX-11 could pull down endogenous ER in ZR-75 nuclear extracts.
source: We then demonstrated that biotinylated ERX-11 could pull down endogenous ER in ZR-75 nuclear extracts (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ERX-11 directly interacts with ER, both as purified protein and within a cellular context.
source: These data indicate that ERX-11 directly interact with ER, both as purified protein and within a cellular context.
evidence: This is supported by multiple pulldown assays with purified protein and cellular extracts shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Immunoprecipitation mass spectrometric (IPMS) analyses of biotinylated ERX-11 pulldown in MCF-7 cells identified ER as one of the top ERX-11 interactors.
source: Unbiased evaluation, using immunoprecipitation mass spectrometric (IPMS) analyses of the biotinylated ERX-11 pulldown in MCF-7 cells, identified ER as one of the top ERX-11 interactors (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: ERX-11-binding proteins were involved in the activation of transcriptional regulation.
source: Pathways analysis revealed that ERX-11-binding proteins were involved in the activation of transcriptional regulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pathway analysis of mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERX-11 pulldown included a number of proteins other than ER, including a weak affinity for the progesterone receptor (PGR) and several ER-associated proteins.
source: Importantly, ERX-11 pulldown included a number of proteins other than ER, including a weak affinity for the progesterone receptor (PGR) and several ER-associated proteins (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: Immunoprecipitation analyses in MCF-7 cells validated the strong affinity of ERX-11 for ER, and weak affinity for the PR-A isoform but not GR, AR or PR-B isoforms.
source: Immunoprecipitation analyses in MCF-7 cells validated the strong affinity of ERX-11 for ER, and weak affinity for the PR-A isoform but not GR, AR or PR-B isoforms (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis of pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The interaction between ER and ERX-11 within cells was partially disrupted by high doses of tamoxifen.
source: The interaction between ER and ERX-11 within the cells was partially disrupted by high doses of tamoxifen (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the tamoxifen-resistant cell line MCF-7-TamR, even high doses of tamoxifen could not disrupt the interaction between ERX-11 and ER.
source: Further, in the tamoxifen-resistant cell line, MCF-7-TamR, even high doses of tamoxifen could not disrupt the interaction between ERX-11 and ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays in tamoxifen-resistant cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: ERX-11 interacts with the GST-AF2 domain of ER but not with the GST-AF1 or GST-DNA-binding domain of ER.
source: Using GST-fused ER domain constructs, we validated that ERX-11 interact with the GST-AF2 domain of ER but not with the GST-AF1 or GST-DNA-binding domain of ER (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST pulldown assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ER-AF2 interaction with ERX-11 was disrupted by tamoxifen but not ICI.
source: Further, ER-AF2 interaction with ERX-11 was disrupted by tamoxifen but not ICI (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays with the AF2 domain shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ERX-11 significantly disrupted the interactions of 91 nuclear ER-binding proteins with ER in MCF-7 cells.
source: Using an unbiased approach with IPMS, we showed that ERX-11 significantly disrupted the interactions of 91 nuclear ER-binding proteins with ER in MCF-7 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), including well-characterized ER coregulators, such as SRC1, SRC3, and PELP1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ERX-11 disrupted interactions with well-characterized ER coregulators, such as SRC1, SRC3, and PELP1.
source: Using an unbiased approach with IPMS, we showed that ERX-11 significantly disrupted the interactions of 91 nuclear ER-binding proteins with ER in MCF-7 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), including well-characterized ER coregulators, such as SRC1, SRC3, and PELP1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Proteins whose interactions with ER were disrupted by ERX-11 may be involved in a number of critical cellular pathways including transcription, cell cycle and regulation of cell death.
source: Global analyses revealed that these proteins may be involved in a number of critical cellular pathways including transcription, cell cycle and regulation of cell death (Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pathway analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: IPMS studies in ZR-75 cells showed a significant overlap with MCF-7 cells in the coregulators disrupted by ERX-11.
source: These findings were validated by IPMS studies in ZR-75 cells, which showed a significant overlap with MCF-7 cells in the coregulators disrupted by ERX-11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Of the top 10 coregulators whose interactions with ER were negatively influenced by ERX-11, five contained LXXLL motifs with serine at i-3/4 and i+7/8 flanking position of the LXXLL motifs.
source: Of the top 10 coregulators, whose interactions with ER were negatively influenced by ERX-11, five contained LXXLL motifs with serine at i-3/4 and i+7/8 flanking position of the LXXLL motifs Table 3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Table 3 (which appears to be Table 6 in the manuscript).

claim: In MDA-MB-231 TNBC model cells, biotinylated ERX-11 was able to stringently interact only with a small number of proteins (n = 8).
source: Interestingly in the MDA-MB-231 TNBC model cells, we found that biotinylated ERX-11 was able to stringently interact only with a small number of proteins (n = 8) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis in ER-negative cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A majority of ER-binding proteins disrupted by ERX-11 in MCF-7 cells were also blocked by tamoxifen (55/88 proteins or 62.5%).
source: In MCF-7 cells, a majority of ER-binding proteins disrupted by ERX-11 were also blocked by tamoxifen (55/88 proteins or 62.5%) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A significant number of ER-binding proteins were disrupted by ERX-11 but not tamoxifen (33/88 or 37.5%).
source: Importantly, a significant number of ER-binding proteins were disrupted by ERX-11 but not tamoxifen (33/88 or 37.5%) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation studies validated that endogenous complexes containing ER and coregulator PELP1 form in MCF-7 cells and that ERX-11 disrupts the formation of these complexes.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation studies validated that endogenous complexes containing ER and coregulator PELP1 do form in MCF-7 cells and that ERX-11 disrupts the formation of these complexes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Proximity ligation assays confirmed the disruption of the endogenous interaction between ER and several coregulators including PELP1, SRC1 and SRC3.
source: Proximity ligation assays confirmed the disruption of the endogenous interaction between ER and several coregulators including PELP1, SRC1 and SRC3 (Figure 2I, quantitation in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assays shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ERX-11 has no effect on ER interaction with ARID1B.
source: In contrast, ERX-11 has no effect on ER interaction with ARID1B (Figure 2I, quantitation in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assays shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Using an in vivo structural complementation NanoBiT assay, the direct interaction between ER and PELP1 was enhanced by E2 treatment and ERX-11 significantly reduced the interaction between ER and PELP1.
source: Using an in vivo structural complementation NanoBiT assay, we found that the direct interaction between ER and PELP1 was enhanced by E2 treatment and that ERX-11 significantly reduced the interaction between ER and PELP1 (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NanoBiT luciferase assays shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ERX-11 failed to reduce the ERE-Luc reporter activity driven by a ERα-VP16 chimera that does not require AF-2.
source: To confirm the specificity of ERX-11 for the ER AF-2 domain, we demonstrated using reporter-based assays, that ERX-11 failed to reduce the ERE-Luc reporter activity driven by a ERα-VP16 chimera that does not require AF-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: ERX-11 lacks AF1 agonist activity in Ishikawa endometrial cancer cell line.
source: Evaluation with an endometrial cancer cell line Ishikawa, which exhibits agonist activity via AF1, revealed that ERX-11 lacks AF1 agonist activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays in Ishikawa cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: ERX-11 blocks signaling driven by functional AF2 domain but not by AF1 domain.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that the ERX-11 block signaling driven by functional AF2 domain but not by AF1 domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay data with AF1 and AF2 constructs.

claim: Biotinylated ERX-11 was able to pull down both the wild-type ER and the L540Q point mutant ER.
source: Biotinylated ERX-11 was able to pull down both the wild-type ER and the L540Q point mutant ER (which retains E2 binding and does not interact with SRC1) and these interactions were not affected by tamoxifen (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays with ER mutants shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The interaction between biotinylated ERX-11 and wild-type ER or L540Q mutant ER was not affected by tamoxifen.
source: Biotinylated ERX-11 was able to pull down both the wild-type ER and the L540Q point mutant ER (which retains E2 binding and does not interact with SRC1) and these interactions were not affected by tamoxifen (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ERX-11 binds strongly to ER▲12 mutant (helix 12 deleted ER).
source: Interestingly, the ERX-11 binds strongly to ER▲12 mutant (helix 12 deleted ER) and this binding is blocked efficiently by tamoxifen (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays with ER▲12 mutant shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The binding of ERX-11 to ER▲12 mutant is blocked efficiently by tamoxifen.
source: Interestingly, the ERX-11 binds strongly to ER▲12 mutant (helix 12 deleted ER) and this binding is blocked efficiently by tamoxifen (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The presence of helix 12 may regulate the conformation of the binding pocket and account for differences in the binding of ERX-11 and tamoxifen to ER.
source: These data suggest that the presence of helix 12 may regulate the conformation of the binding pocket and account for differences in the binding of ERX-11 and tamoxifen to ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of tamoxifen on ERX-11 binding to wild-type ER versus ER▲12.

claim: Removal of helix 12 enables access of ERX-11 to the same binding pocket as tamoxifen.
source: Our data would suggest that removal of helix 12 enables access of ERX-11 to the same binding pocket as tamoxifen and may reflect the in vitro data, where tamoxifen and ERX-11 compete efficiently for ER binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition data with ER▲12 mutant.

claim: Neither GDC-0810 nor AZD-9496 were able to block ERX-11 binding to ER or its mutants.
source: In contrast, neither GDC-0810 nor AZD-9496 were able to block ERX-11 binding to ER or its mutants, suggesting that their binding to ER occurs through distinct pockets (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: GDC-0810 and AZD-9496 binding to ER occurs through distinct pockets from ERX-11.
source: In contrast, neither GDC-0810 nor AZD-9496 were able to block ERX-11 binding to ER or its mutants, suggesting that their binding to ER occurs through distinct pockets (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of competition between SERDs and ERX-11.

claim: Tamoxifen fails to dislodge ERX-11 from ER in competition assays.
source: In competition assays, tamoxifen fails to dislodge ERX-11 from ER (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Increasing concentrations of tamoxifen is only able to dislodge ERX-11 from ER▲12 mutant at higher concentrations.
source: Increasing concentrations of tamoxifen is only able to dislodge ERX-11 from ER▲12 mutant at higher concentrations, suggesting that ERX-11 interaction with ER is through a second binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response competition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claim: ERX-11 interaction with ER is through a second binding site.
source: Increasing concentrations of tamoxifen is only able to dislodge ERX-11 from ER▲12 mutant at higher concentrations, suggesting that ERX-11 interaction with ER is through a second binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the competition data with ER▲12 mutant.

claim: Introduction of either ER, ER▲12 or ER-L540Q into MDA-MB-231 cells restored ERX-11 growth inhibitory activity in non-responsive MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Further, using an ER restoration model, MTT cell viability assays revealed that introduction of either ER, ER▲12 or ER-L540Q into MDA-MB-231 cells, restored ERX-11 growth inhibitory activity in non-responsive MDA-MB-231 cells. These results further underscore the importance of ER in ERX-11 mode of action (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays in ER-reconstituted cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The importance of ER in ERX-11 mode of action is underscored by ER restoration experiments.
source: Further, using an ER restoration model, MTT cell viability assays revealed that introduction of either ER, ER▲12 or ER-L540Q into MDA-MB-231 cells, restored ERX-11 growth inhibitory activity in non-responsive MDA-MB-231 cells. These results further underscore the importance of ER in ERX-11 mode of action (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of ERX-11 activity upon ER expression in ER-negative cells.

claim: In the agonist-bound conformation (3ERD.pdb), ERX-11 can be modeled to make hydrophobic contact with the AF2 site with its two isobutyl side chain groups.
source: In the agonist-bound conformation (3ERD.pdb), helix 12 is relocated and forms a hydrophobic cleft (i.e. AF2-binding site) that is surrounded by helices 3, 4, 5 and 12: ERX-11 can be modeled to make hydrophobic contact with the AF2 site with its two isobutyl side chain groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(A)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: The hydroxyl group of ERX-11 may interact with a residue near AF2 domain.
source: In addition, the hydroxyl group of ERX-11 may interact with a residue near AF2 domain. These data suggest that ERX-11 interacts with ER LBD differently than the agonist.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling predictions.

claim: ERX-11 interacts with ER LBD differently than the agonist.
source: In addition, the hydroxyl group of ERX-11 may interact with a residue near AF2 domain. These data suggest that ERX-11 interacts with ER LBD differently than the agonist.
evidence: This is inferred from the docking simulations.

claim: In the antagonist-bound conformation (3ERT.pdb), ERX-11 may interact with an alternate pocket formed by helices 5, 11 and 12.
source: In the antagonist-bound conformation (3ERT.pdb), 4-hydroxytamoxifen induces conformational change and makes helix 12 occupy the AF2-binding site, blocking both coactivator and corepressor binding: here, ERX-11 may interact with an alternate pocket formed by helices 5, 11 and 12, as shown in the Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(B).
evidence: This is based on molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: The secondary binding site of ERX-11 on ER may be stabilized by coregulators in a cellular context.
source: These data could explain why the interaction between ERX-11 and purified ER could be blocked by tamoxifen. However, in a cellular context, tamoxifen cannot block ERX-11 binding to ER suggesting that the secondary binding site of ERX-11 on ER may be stabilized by coregulators.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differences between in vitro and cellular competition experiments.

claim: Docking simulation of ERX-11 on human ERα with affinity-tagged corepressor peptide (2JFA.pdb) showed that ERX-11 can still bind to the AF2 domain.
source: Docking simulation of ERX-11 on human ERα with affinity-tagged corepressor peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(C))(2JFA.pdb) or rat ERβ crystal structure with ICI bound (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(D))(1HJ1.pdb) showed that ERX-11 can still bind to the AF2 domain, in a similar manner as it does when the ligand is bound.
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Docking simulation of ERX-11 on rat ERβ crystal structure with ICI bound (1HJ1.pdb) showed that ERX-11 can still bind to the AF2 domain.
source: Docking simulation of ERX-11 on human ERα with affinity-tagged corepressor peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(C))(2JFA.pdb) or rat ERβ crystal structure with ICI bound (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A(D))(1HJ1.pdb) showed that ERX-11 can still bind to the AF2 domain, in a similar manner as it does when the ligand is bound.
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Docking simulations support the biochemical findings that ICI does not block ERX-11 interaction with ER.
source: These data further support our biochemical findings that ICI does not block ERX-11 interaction with ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the docking simulations and experimental data.

claim: Two isobutyl groups of ERX-11 may dock into the AF2 binding site.
source: Detailed evaluation showed that (1L2I.pdb) two isobutyl groups of ERX-11 may dock into the AF2 binding site (black dashed box) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This is based on detailed molecular modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B.

claim: The hydroxyl group of ERX-11 may interact with Gln375 of helix five through a hydrogen bond.
source: The hydroxyl group of ERX-11 may interact with Gln375 of the helix five through a hydrogen bond.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling predictions.

claim: The carboxamide group of ERX-11 was docked into a pocket formed with Gln542, Asp545 and Ala546 on helix 12.
source: The carboxamide group of ERX-11 was docked into a pocket formed with Gln542, Asp545 and Ala546 on the helix 12.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling predictions.

claim: Docking experiment on ER crystal structures without helix 12 (3ERT.pdb and 5ACC.pdb) showed that ERX-11 was found to bind to the tamoxifen-binding site in the ER▲12.
source: Additional docking experiment on ER crystal structures without helix 12 (3ERT.pdb and 5ACC.pdb) showed that ERX-11 was found to bind to the tamoxifen-binding site in the ER▲12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(A)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C.

claim: The superimposition of tamoxifen and ERX-11 clearly shows the overlap of their binding sites in ER▲12.
source: The superimposition of tamoxifen (red) and ERX-11 (green) clearly shows the overlap of their binding sites (3ERT.pdb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(B)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C.

claim: The overlap of tamoxifen and ERX-11 binding sites in ER▲12 may explain the experimental results showing the competition of tamoxifen with ERX-11 on ER▲12.
source: This may explain our experimental results showing the competition of tamoxifen with ERX-11 on ER▲12.
evidence: This is inferred from the docking simulations and experimental data.

claim: In the presence of SERDs, ERX-11 can bind to the AF2 domain.
source: In the presence of SERDs, ERX-11 can bind to the AF2 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(C), which do not overlap with the binding site of SERDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(D)) (5ACC.pdb).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C.

claim: ERX-11 binding site does not overlap with the binding site of SERDs.
source: In the presence of SERDs, ERX-11 can bind to the AF2 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(C), which do not overlap with the binding site of SERDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C(D)) (5ACC.pdb).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C.

claim: ERX-11 altered the expression of 880 E2-regulated genes (p<0.01) in ZR-75 cells compared to vehicle control.
source: RNA-seq analyses revealed that ERX-11 altered the expression of 880 E2-regulated genes (p<0.01) in ZR-75 cells compared to vehicle control (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Using stringent cutoffs (p<0.01 and RPKM FC > 1.5), ERX-11 down-regulated more genes (669) than upregulated (211).
source: Using stringent cutoffs (p<0.01 and RPKM FC > 1.5), ERX-11 down-regulated more genes (669) than upregulated (211) as evidenced by the volcano plot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) (complete list at GEO database, accession number GSE75664).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses validated the expression of the top down-regulated genes.
source: RT-qPCR analyses validated the expression of the top down-regulated (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and up-regulated genes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses validated the expression of the top up-regulated genes.
source: RT-qPCR analyses validated the expression of the top down-regulated (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and up-regulated genes (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR validation shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) confirmed the correlation between ERX-11–regulated genes and both the tamoxifen-responsive and E2-responsive genes set.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) confirmed the correlation between ERX-11–regulated genes and both the tamoxifen-responsive and E2-responsive genes set (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: ERX-11-regulated genes correlated well with signatures of early and late response E2 targets as well as genes driven by consensus ER motifs.
source: In addition, ERX-11-regulated genes correlated well with signatures of early and late response E2 targets as well as genes driven by consensus ER motifs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) revealed that ERX-11 significantly down-regulated genes involved in ER-signaling, breast cancer, cell cycle, and MAPK signaling.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) revealed that ERX-11 significantly down-regulated genes involved in ER-signaling, breast cancer, cell cycle, and MAPK signaling (Table 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pathway analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: ERX-11 upregulated gene set positively correlated with apoptotic genes on GSEA analyses.
source: ERX-11 upregulated gene set positively correlated with apoptotic genes, on GSEA analyses (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ERX-11 but not tamoxifen or ICI-treatment-induced apoptosis in ZR-75 cells as shown by induction of caspase 3/7 activity.
source: Importantly, ERX-11 but not tamoxifen or ICI-treatment-induced apoptosis in ZR-75 (Figure 3I) and in T-47D cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) as shown by induction of caspase 3/7 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by caspase 3/7 activity assays shown in Figure 3I.

claim: ERX-11 but not tamoxifen or ICI-treatment-induced apoptosis in T-47D cells as shown by induction of caspase 3/7 activity.
source: Importantly, ERX-11 but not tamoxifen or ICI-treatment-induced apoptosis in ZR-75 (Figure 3I) and in T-47D cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) as shown by induction of caspase 3/7 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by caspase 3/7 activity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Apoptosis by ERX-11 can be seen as early as 24 hr, however, the effect is more pronounced at 72 hr.
source: Apoptosis can be seen as early as 24 hr, however, the effect is more pronounced at 72 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course caspase 3/7 activity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ERX-11 both reduces the expression of genes involved in proliferation and enhances expression of genes that promote apoptosis.
source: These results suggest that ERX-11 both reduces the expression of genes involved in proliferation and enhances expression of genes that promote apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq and pathway analysis data.

claim: ERX-11 significantly reduced the E2-induced ERE-Luc reporter gene activity in ZR-75 cells in a similar fashion as tamoxifen.
source: Using ERE-Luc reporter based transcription assays, we found that ERX-11 significantly reduced the E2-induced ERE-Luc reporter gene activity in ZR-75 cells in a similar fashion as tamoxifen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In HEK-293T cells, expression of AIB1 and SRC1 enhanced ER-driven ERE-Luc reporter activity and was blocked by both tamoxifen and ERX-11 in a ligand-dependent manner.
source: In HEK-293T cells, expression of AIB1 and SRC1 enhanced ER-driven ERE-Luc reporter activity and was blocked by both tamoxifen and ERX-11 in both a ligand-dependent (Figure 4B) and ligand-independent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In HEK-293T cells, expression of AIB1 and SRC1 enhanced ER-driven ERE-Luc reporter activity and was blocked by both tamoxifen and ERX-11 in a ligand-independent manner.
source: In HEK-293T cells, expression of AIB1 and SRC1 enhanced ER-driven ERE-Luc reporter activity and was blocked by both tamoxifen and ERX-11 in both a ligand-dependent (Figure 4B) and ligand-independent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ZR-75 cells stably overexpressing either PELP1 or AIB-1 were responsive to ERX-11.
source: Further, ZR-75 cells stably overexpressing either PELP1 or AIB-1 were responsive to ERX-11 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability and reporter assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ERX-11 interferes with both ligand-dependent and ligand-independent transcriptional function of ER.
source: These results indicate that ERX-11 interferes with both ligand-dependent and ligand-independent transcriptional function of ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay data with and without ligand.

claim: ERX-11 treatment significantly blocked ER recruitment to canonical ER target gene promoters following E2 treatment.
source: Using chromatin immunoprecipitation studies, we found that ERX-11 treatment significantly blocked ER recruitment to canonical ER target gene promoters following E2 treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ERX-11 did not affect AR recruitment to AR target genes.
source: In contrast, ERX-11 did not affect AR recruitment to AR target genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ERX-11 efficiently blocks the dimerization of ER.
source: Using the NanoBiT assay, we demonstrated that ERX-11 efficiently blocks the dimerization of ER (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NanoBiT assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ERX-11 did not affect AR dimerization.
source: In contrast, ERX-11 did not affect AR dimerization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NanoBiT assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ERX-11 was unable to influence the EDC-mediated non-genomic activation of the Src, AKT and MAPK pathways.
source: Using E2 dendrimer conjugates (EDC), that are potent in activating ER non-genomic signaling but not ER genomic signaling (Chakravarty et al., 2010), we showed that ERX-11 was unable to influence the EDC-mediated non-genomic activation of the Src, AKT and MAPK pathways (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis of signaling pathways shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ERX-11 treatment only modestly altered the stability of ER within 24 hr in ZR-75 and T-47D cells.
source: A detailed time course evaluation showed that ERX-11 treatment only modestly altered the stability of ER within 24 hr in ZR-75 and T-47D cells (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot time-course analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: After several days of ERX-11 treatment, decreased ER levels were detected.
source: However, similar to its inhibitory activity on ER transcription, after several days of ERX-11 treatment, decreased ER levels were detected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: RTqPCR results showed that ERX-11 reduce the ER transcript levels under conditions of long-term treatment (7 days).
source: Accordingly, RTqPCR results showed that ERX-11 reduce the ER transcript levels under conditions of long-term treatment (7 days). These results reflect the inhibition of ER signaling indirectly affected autoregulation of ER transcript by E2-ER signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The reduction in ER transcript levels by ERX-11 reflects the inhibition of ER signaling indirectly affecting autoregulation of ER transcript by E2-ER signaling.
source: Accordingly, RTqPCR results showed that ERX-11 reduce the ER transcript levels under conditions of long-term treatment (7 days). These results reflect the inhibition of ER signaling indirectly affected autoregulation of ER transcript by E2-ER signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the RT-qPCR data and knowledge of ER autoregulation.

claim: No overt signs of toxicity were detected after 14 days of treatment of C57BL/6 mice with 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day of ERX-11 via oral gavage.
source: We detected no overt signs of toxicity after 14 days of treatment of C57BL/6 mice (n = 3) with 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day of ERX-11 via oral gavage.
evidence: This is based on toxicity studies in mice.

claim: ERX-11 treatment neither caused weight loss nor have uterotrophic effects or any observable hematologic, liver and kidney abnormalities.
source: ERX-11 treatment neither caused weight loss nor have uterotrophic effects or any observable hematologic, liver and kidney abnormalities (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on toxicity studies in mice.

claim: The maximum tolerated dose of ERX-11 was designated as 100 mg/kg.
source: We designated our highest dose (100 mg/kg) as the maximum tolerated dose and used 10% of this dose (10 mg/kg/day) for testing as therapeutic dose, so that we would have at least a 10:1 therapeutic to toxicity ratio.
evidence: This is based on the toxicity study design.

claim: ERX-11 treatment resulted in significantly smaller ZR-75 xenograft tumors (63% reduction compared to control).
source: Established ZR-75 xenografts (n = 8 tumors/group) in the mammary fat pad of nude mice were randomized to feed via oral gavage 5 days/week with either 10 mg/kg ERX-11 or vehicle (30% Captisol). ERX-11 treatment resulted in significantly smaller tumors (63% reduction compared to control) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ERX-11–treated ZR-75 xenograft tumors exhibited less proliferation (Ki67 staining) than controls.
source: ERX-11–treated tumors exhibited less proliferation (Ki67 staining), and more apoptosis (TUNEL and caspase-3 staining) than controls (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IHC analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: ERX-11–treated ZR-75 xenograft tumors exhibited more apoptosis (TUNEL and caspase-3 staining) than controls.
source: ERX-11–treated tumors exhibited less proliferation (Ki67 staining), and more apoptosis (TUNEL and caspase-3 staining) than controls (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IHC analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: ERX-11 treatment group had lower ER but similar PELP1 protein expression levels within the ZR-75 xenograft tumor, compared to control.
source: Further, ERX-11 treatment group had lower ER but similar PELP1 protein expression levels within the tumor, compared to control (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IHC analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mice body weights in the control and ERX-11 treated groups were similar in ZR-75 xenograft study.
source: The mice body weights in the control and ERX-11 treated groups were similar (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by body weight measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mice treated with ERX-11 exhibited no uterotrophic effects, no changes in ovary, liver and kidney gross morphology on H and E staining, or acute phase injury to liver and kidney.
source: Mice treated with ERX-11 exhibited no uterotrophic effects, no changes in ovary, liver and kidney gross morphology on H and E staining, or acute phase injury to liver and kidney (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: ERX-11 is a potent inhibitor of the growth of ER-positive breast tumors in vivo with no overt signs of toxicity in mice.
source: These data indicate that ERX-11 is a potent inhibitor of the growth of ER-positive breast tumors in vivo with no overt signs of toxicity in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft and toxicity data.

claim: Oral administration of ERX-11 dramatically limited the proliferation of rapidly progressing D2A1 syngeneic tumors.
source: D2A1 ER-positive breast cancer xenografts were established in a syngeneic BALB/c model system with an intact immune system. In D2A1 model cells, cellular gene int-5/aromatase in BALB/c mammary alveolar hyperplastic nodule (D2 HAN/D2 tumor cells) is activated as a result of mouse mammary tumor virus integration within the 3' untranslated region of the aromatase gene. Thus, these models also have ability to synthesize local estrogen via aromatase induction. Further, this model express ER, and represent a model of intra-tumoral estrogen-driven mammary cancer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B(A,C). D2A1 cells are responsive to antiestrogen treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B(B). Oral administration of ERX-11 dramatically limited the proliferation of these rapidly progressing tumors (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth measurements in syngeneic models shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The proliferative indices of ERX-11-treated D2A1 tumors were significantly lower than controls.
source: The proliferative indices of ERX-11-treated tumors were significantly lower than controls (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), while the apoptotic indices were higher than control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ki67 staining shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The apoptotic indices of ERX-11-treated D2A1 tumors were higher than control.
source: The proliferative indices of ERX-11-treated tumors were significantly lower than controls (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), while the apoptotic indices were higher than control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TUNEL staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No overt signs of toxicity was noted in D2A1 syngeneic model mice treated with ERX-11.
source: Again, no overt signs of toxicity was noted in these mice; specifically, no enlargement of the spleen or evidence of immune complex deposition within the kidneys was detected (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on toxicity assessment in syngeneic models.

claim: No enlargement of the spleen or evidence of immune complex deposition within the kidneys was detected in D2A1 syngeneic model mice treated with ERX-11.
source: Again, no overt signs of toxicity was noted in these mice; specifically, no enlargement of the spleen or evidence of immune complex deposition within the kidneys was detected (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on toxicity assessment in syngeneic models.

claim: ERX-11 was potent in blocking proliferation of ZR-75 cells stably overexpressing AIB-1 and PELP1.
source: To evaluate the effect of ERX-11 on coregulator-driven proliferation, we used ZR-75 cells stably overexpressing AIB-1 and PELP1. While these modified ZR-75 cells are highly proliferative (Figure 4D), ERX-11 was potent in blocking their proliferation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ERX-11 was potent (73% reduction in tumor volume compared to control) against the growth of MCF-7-PELP1 xenografts.
source: ERX-11 was potent (73% reduction in tumor volume compared to control) against the growth of MCF-7-PELP1 xenografts, which overexpress PELP1 (3-fold higher than parental MCF-7) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IHC analysis of ERX-11 treated MCF-7-PELP1 tumors showed decreased Ki-67 staining.
source: IHC analysis of ERX-11 treated tumors showed decreased Ki-67 staining (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IHC analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were resistant to tamoxifen (MCF-7-TamR).
source: Importantly, ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were either resistant to tamoxifen (MCF-7-TamR, Figure 6A, or MCF-7-HER2, Figure 6B) or to letrozole (MCF-7-LTLT, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were resistant to tamoxifen (MCF-7-HER2).
source: Importantly, ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were either resistant to tamoxifen (MCF-7-TamR, Figure 6A, or MCF-7-HER2, Figure 6B) or to letrozole (MCF-7-LTLT, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were resistant to letrozole (MCF-7-LTLT).
source: Importantly, ERX-11 had activity against ER-driven breast cancer cell lines that were either resistant to tamoxifen (MCF-7-TamR, Figure 6A, or MCF-7-HER2, Figure 6B) or to letrozole (MCF-7-LTLT, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In therapy-resistant cell lines, ERX-11 was still able to interact with the ER, both in the absence and presence of tamoxifen.
source: In these cell lines, ERX-11 was still able to interact with the ER, both in the absence and presence of tamoxifen (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays in resistant cell lines shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In contrast to SERD (ICI), which had limited activity on the tamoxifen resistant cell lines, ERX-11 had potent activity.
source: In contrast to SERD (ICI), which had limited activity on the tamoxifen resistant cell lines, ERX-11 had potent activity (Figure 6A) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays comparing ERX-11 and ICI shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ERX-11 was potent against the growth of MCF-7-LTLT xenografts.
source: ERX-11 was potent against the growth of MCF-7-LTLT xenografts (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: IHC analysis of ERX-11-treated MCF-7-LTLT tumors showed decreased Ki-67 staining.
source: IHC analysis of ERX-11-treated tumors showed decreased Ki-67 staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IHC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Using biotinylated ERX-11, ERX-11 interacts directly with ESR1-MT (ESR1-MT-D538G, ESR1-MT-Y537S), with high affinity comparable to the affinity to WT-ER.
source: We then evaluated the effect of ERX-11 against two prevalent ER mutants (MT-ESR1-Y537S, MT-ESR1-D538G) (Toy et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014; Merenbakh-Lamin et al., 2013). Using biotinylated ERX-11, we showed that ERX-11 interacts directly with ESR1-MT (ESR1-MT-D538G, ESR1-MT-Y537S), with high affinity comparable to the affinity to WT-ER (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pulldown assays with ER mutants shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Using CRISPR/Cas9, ER was knocked down in ZR-75 cells and then stably transfected with WT-ESR1 or MT-ESR1 (Y537S, and D538G).
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9, we knocked down ER in ZR-75 cells and then stably transfected with WT-ESR1 or MT-ESR1 (Y537S, and D538G).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to generate model cell lines.

claim: ESR1-MT expressing cells showed higher rates of proliferation than WT-ESR1-expressing cells.
source: While ESR1-MT expressing cells showed higher rates of proliferation than WT-ESR1-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), they were still inhibited by ERX-11 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ESR1-MT expressing cells were still inhibited by ERX-11.
source: While ESR1-MT expressing cells showed higher rates of proliferation than WT-ESR1-expressing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), they were still inhibited by ERX-11 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The ability of ESR1-MT to drive ligand-independent transcription from an ERE-Luc reporter was efficiently blocked by ERX-11.
source: Further the ability of these ESR1-MT to drive ligand-independent transcription from an ERE-Luc reporter was also efficiently blocked by ERX-11 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays shown in Figure 6H.

claim: ESR1-MT expressing cells were resistant to tamoxifen, however, were sensitive to ERX-11-mediated growth inhibition.
source: Further, these ESR1-MT expressing cells were resistant to tamoxifen, however, were sensitive to ERX-11-mediated growth inhibition (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Oral ERX-11 administration had significant activity against the growth of ZR-75-ESR1MT-Y537S xenografts in vivo.
source: Further, oral ERX-11 administration had significant activity against the growth of ZR-75-ESR1MT-Y537S xenografts in vivo (Figure 6J), with significant reduction in proliferative indices (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth measurements shown in Figure 6J.

claim: ERX-11 treatment of ZR-75-ESR1MT-Y537S xenografts resulted in significant reduction in proliferative indices.
source: Further, oral ERX-11 administration had significant activity against the growth of ZR-75-ESR1MT-Y537S xenografts in vivo (Figure 6J), with significant reduction in proliferative indices (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ki67 staining shown in Figure 6K.

claim: ERX-11 is effective against breast tumors driven by mutant ESR1.
source: These data support the efficacy of ERX-11 against breast tumors driven by mutant ESR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data with ESR1 mutant cell lines and xenografts.

claim: Incubation of ERX-11 with ER-positive breast tumor samples dramatically decreased their proliferation in 11/12 patients (Ki67 staining) compared to untreated controls.
source: Incubation of ERX-11 with ER-positive breast tumor samples (patient characteristics detailed in Table 4) dramatically decreased their proliferation in 11/12 patients (Ki67 staining) compared to untreated controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ki67 staining in patient-derived explants shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ERX-11 treatment significantly reduced the ER staining in 12/12 ER-positive tumors in patient-derived explants.
source: Further, ERX-11 treatment significantly reduced the ER staining (Figure 7C), but not PELP1 staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) in 12/12 ER-positive tumors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ER staining in patient-derived explants shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ERX-11 treatment did not reduce PELP1 staining in 12/12 ER-positive tumors in patient-derived explants.
source: Further, ERX-11 treatment significantly reduced the ER staining (Figure 7C), but not PELP1 staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) in 12/12 ER-positive tumors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PELP1 staining in patient-derived explants shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERX-11 treatment had no effect on the proliferation on 6/6 triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) tumors in patient-derived explants.
source: Importantly, ERX-11 treatment had no effect on the proliferation on 6/6 triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) tumors (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ki67 staining in TNBC patient-derived explants shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ERX-11 has the potential to selectively influence the growth of human breast tumors expressing ER.
source: These results suggest that ERX-11 has the potential to selectively influence the growth of human breast tumors expressing ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the patient-derived explant data showing selective activity in ER-positive tumors.
